PRECLINICAL MODELS 488

Traditional epidemiologic approaches are only a first step of many in the process of elucidating 489

the role of inter-organ crosstalk in heart failure. Whereas studies examining circulating 490

biomarkers provide invaluable insights into the mechanisms underlying heart failure, pre-clinical 491

models offer the opportunity to test these hypotheses in a mechanistic context. In addition, 492

animal models may interrogate established associations between the 'common soil' of underlying 493

cardiometabolic comorbidities and the onset of more complex organ failure, dissecting the stages 494

of disease progression and potential causality106,107. These studies take on particular importance 495

in the setting of multi-morbidity and the bidirectional risks between heart failure and other 496

chronic diseases, as described above. In this section, we will provide an overview of the existing 497

pre-clinical models of heart failure, including both HFrEF and HFpEF, and discuss opportunities 498

to develop future models to best capture the spectrum of inter-organ crosstalk in HF development 499

and progression. 500

501

Preclinical Models of HFrEF 502

Pathophysiological Mechanisms of HFrEF 503

HFrEF, typically caused by hypertension or myocardial infarction, is marked by impairment of 504

the ejection of blood108. The subsequent compensatory neurohormonal activation, such as via the 505

renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system, further 506

exacerbate HF symptoms109. Resulting pathophysiology involves changes in myocardial 507

remodeling, including ventricular dilation, fibrosis, and alterations in myocyte function110. These 508

mechanisms lead to additional decrease in the ability of the heart to pump blood efficiently, 509

contributing to hallmark symptoms of HFrEF, such as shortness of breath, fatigue, and fluid 510

retention. Here, we provide a brief overview of HFrEF mechanisms and models, focusing more 511

on HFpEF. 512

513

Defining HFrEF in Animal Models 514

Defining HFrEF in animal models is relatively straightforward as compared with HFpEF, 515

primarily relying on transthoracic echocardiographic indices such as reduced ejection fraction, 516

fractional shortening, and increased LV mass. Pathological assessment involves evaluating tissue 517

morphology, including features such as LV dilation, altered LV wall thickness, concentric or 518

eccentric LV hypertrophy, cardiomyocyte loss, and fibrosis, coupled with molecular markers of 519

fetal gene program re-activation. 520

521

Common HFrEF Models 522

The transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model is widely used for studying pathophysiological 523

mechanisms of HFrEF, first introduced in 1991 by Rockman and colleagues111,112. The primary 524

procedure involves anesthetizing the mouse, performing a thoracotomy to expose and isolate the 525

aorta, and then ligating it to create an artificial constriction with a diameter of approximately 0.4 526

mm113. This increases afterload on the left ventricle, promoting ventricular hypertrophy and 527

fibrosis, contractile dysfunction, and triggering a certain degree of inflammation. Ultimately, 528

these changes lead to ventricular dilation and the development of HFrEF112. The phenotype can 529

vary depending on specific aspects of the surgical procedure (e.g. positioning of the surgical 530

needle that dictates the degree of stenosis), the species and strain of experimental animals and the 531

timing of the intervention112,114. 532

533


<!-- Page 14 -->


Coronary artery ligation is another commonly used approach for inducing HFrEF. The principle 534

behind this model is surgically occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery to induce 535

myocardial infarction, causing myocardial cell death artificially, leading to impaired myocardial 536

contractile function and left ventricular remodeling, hallmarks of clinical HFrEF115-117.  Beyond 537

that, in most high-income countries, due to the widespread use of coronary reperfusion 538

approaches, acute myocardial infarction is typically followed by emergent reperfusion therapy, 539

and simple myocardial infarction is less commonly seen. Instead, the combination of ischemia 540

coupled with reperfusion injury causes damage to myocardial cells, leading to HFrEF118,119. 541

Therefore, a model involving temporary (e.g., 45 minutes) left anterior descending coronary 542

artery occlusion followed by a period of reperfusion (e.g., 24 hours) can be arguably more 543

accurate reflection of the clinical realities experienced by many patients, aligning more closely 544

with the pathophysiological process of HFrEF commonly seen in clinical practice today. 545

Pulmonary artery banding (PAB) can induce right ventricular (RV) dilation, right atrial 546

enlargement, and tricuspid regurgitation, leading to a reduction in RV ejection fraction120. 547

548

CKD models, including angiotensin II (Ang II) infusion, high-salt diet, and unilateral 549

nephrectomy, serve as valuable models for studying HFrEF by replicating the intricate interplay 550

between cardiac and renal dysfunction. Unilateral nephrectomy simulates renal dysfunction by 551

reducing nephron numbers, triggering compensatory mechanisms such as glomerular 552

hyperfiltration, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation, and progressive renal 553

damage. Collectively, these models capture the bidirectional relationship between CKD and 554

HFrEF, enabling researchers to investigate the underlying mechanisms of cardiorenal 555

comorbidities and evaluate therapeutic interventions targeting this complex 556

interconnection121,122. 557

558

Additionally, doxorubicin and alcohol are known to induce systemic damage, thereby mimicking 559

some of the key pathophysiological mechanisms associated with HFrEF. These drugs exert 560

widespread systemic effects that complicate the interpretation of results and reduce the 561

specificity of these models in isolating the cardiac effects of HFrEF121. 562

563

Finally, some studies employ genetically modified mice, such as nesprin-1 and Mybpc3-mutant 564

mice, to model HFrEF. By isolating specific genetic alterations associated with HFrEF, 565

transgenic models contribute to a deeper understanding of the syndrome and help refine 566

treatment approaches123,124. 567

568

Preclinical Models of HFpEF 569

Recently, two diagnostic algorithms—the HFA-PEFF125 and H₂ FPEF126 scores—that 570

incorporate typical clinical manifestations and comorbidities have been introduced to enhance 571

the accuracy of HFpEF diagnosis and prognosis. Although these scores are not perfect, they can 572

be used to evaluate the similarities between human HFpEF and animal models, thereby 573

improving the applicability of preclinical HFpEF models127,128. 574

575

Defining HFpEF in Preclinical Models 576

Pulmonary congestion 577

Wet-to-dry lung weight ratio at sacrifice is a simple index of pulmonary vasculature congestion 578

and helpful for establishing increased LV filling pressures129,130. 579


<!-- Page 15 -->


580

Exercise intolerance 581

Events underlying exercise intolerance in HFpEF are multifactorial, including LVDD, obesity, 582

pulmonary dysfunction, skeletal muscle weakness, and more. Voluntary or forced exercise 583

protocols (e.g. treadmill or swimming exercise) are commonly employed131. 584

585

Increased natriuretic peptide levels 586

Elevated natriuretic peptides, such as BNP and NT-proBNP, are responses to increased LV end- 587

diastolic pressure and wall stress, and are now integral to the diagnostic criteria for HFpEF in 588

humans132,133. Similarly, natriuretic peptide levels can be measured in plasma or LV tissue, where 589

they can afford complementary insights. However, comorbid conditions such as AF, obesity, and 590

kidney dysfunction can impact peptide levels in these models, complicating their interpretation. 591

592

Preserved systolic function 593

Systolic function should be preserved as validated by transthoracic echocardiography. In 594

addition, global longitudinal strain (GLS) is a crucial tool for assessing cardiac contractile 595

function, particularly in HFpEF, where GLS can uncover early functional declines characteristic 596

of HFpEF even when the ejection fraction remains within normal limits. GLS reflects the heart's 597

overall contractile function by measuring contractile strain. It can capture subtle changes in the 598

heart more sensitively than traditional ejection fraction and is highly significant in the early 599

diagnosis of HFpEF134,135. However, GLS results are subject to considerable variability, being 600

heavily influenced by heart rate and loading conditions. 601

602

Impaired diastolic function 603

Diastolic function should be evaluated and quantified by Doppler echocardiography. Elevated 604

E/e’ and diminished E/A ratios in Doppler ultrasound are indicative of LV diastolic dysfunction. 605

These parameters, however, vary across animal models, with E/e′ typically ranging from 10–16 606

and E/A from 1.0–2.5136. Additional markers, such as prolonged isovolumetric relaxation time 607

(IVRT), constant τ (tau), and reduced dP/dtmin, reflect delayed relaxation of LV cardiomyocytes 608

and further support the diagnosis of LVDD136,137. Notably, while E/e′ and E/A are highly heart 609

rate-dependent and can be challenging to measure consistently, IVRT is heart rate-independent, 610

offering a more stable and reliable parameter. 611

612

RPLSR (reverse peak longitudinal strain rate) measures the rate of myocardial deformation 613

during early diastole and serves as a sensitive marker for early-stage LVDD136,137. Like GLS, 614

RPLSR is highly dependent on imaging quality and heart rate, which introduces variability and 615

complicates standardization. 616

617

Hemodynamic assessment 618

Although invasive hemodynamic measurements are considered the gold standard for defining 619

HFpEF, their use in patients is limited due to their invasiveness and associated risks. These 620

procedures are also uncommon in rodent models but are frequently performed in large animal 621

models. Such measurements via LV pressure-volume loops and measurements of pulmonary 622

artery pressure provide valuable information, making them particularly useful as evaluating 623

clinical signs and symptoms in animals is challenging. 624

625


<!-- Page 16 -->


Pathophysiological and Molecular Similarities 626

LA enlargement, LV hypertrophy, and fibrosis 627

Pathological assessment of left atrium (LA) and LV tissue in animal models is required, and 628

concentric LV hypertrophy, fibrosis, LA enlargement, and capillary numbers should be 629

quantified. Post-mortem analysis, including heart weight/body weight and heart weight/tibial 630

length, are good indexes of LV hypertrophy. 631

632

Endothelial Dysfunction & Inflammation 633

Low-grade systemic inflammatory and oxidative stress are common in HFpEF patients as well as 634

in some preclinical models. Detection of inflammatory cell infiltration and molecules, such as 635

nitrosative stress, macrophage infiltration, interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor- 636

α138-142, can provide valuable information regarding molecular events within the models. 637

638

Extra-cardiac Comorbidities 639

Hypertension 640

Blood pressure should be monitored periodically during the study. Invasive hemodynamic 641

assessment or tail-cuff measurements can be adopted. 642

643

Obesity 644

Obesity is central to the HFpEF paradigm. Body weight should be measured regularly 645

throughout the study. Body mass composition should be determined regularly and prior to 646

sacrifice. 647

648

Insulin resistance and diabetes 649

Fasting plasma glucose levels and glycated hemoglobin should be measured during the 650

experiment depending on the context and specific questions being posed. Glucose tolerance and 651

insulin sensitivity can be evaluated using glucose and insulin tolerance tests. 652

653

Renal dysfunction 654

Serum creatine, blood urea nitrogen, urine protein, and kidney histopathology at sacrifice can be 655

useful depending on the specific questions being posed. 656

657

MASLD and atrial fibrillation (AF) 658

AF is a well-known comorbidity for HFpEF and represents an important component of the 659

H2FPEF score126, and MAFLD is also an increasingly recognized comorbidity in HFpEF. 660

Whereas LA enlargement is implicated in HFpEF model assessment, presence/induction of AF, 661

liver fibrosis, or liver dysfunction are not extensively evaluated in HFpEF models currently. 662

Going forward, enhanced emphasis on these disorders will be informative and welcome. 663

664

Preclinical Models of Comorbidities in HF and CMDs 665

In real-world clinical practice, and as elaborated above thus far, HF and its associated metabolic 666

comorbidities do not manifest as isolated components of inter-organ crosstalk, but rather as 667

interconnected and multifaceted conditions53,55,61,88,95. The heterogeneous nature and complex 668

pathophysiology in humans have to be taken into account when creating and validating animal 669

models116,128,136. We advocate for a broader, high-level perspective that synthesizes insights into 670


<!-- Page 17 -->


both HFrEF and HFpEF, culminating in a clear call to action for advancing research and clinical 671

management. 672

673

To better define human HF population, clinical parameters and comorbidity patterns, including 674

epidemiology, symptoms, echocardiography and laboratory indexes, treatment strategies, and 675

prognosis, are being used to cluster HF patients into distinct multimorbidity groups using latent 676

class analysis143-145. The common subgroups: (1) ischemic, often associated with atherosclerosis- 677

related risk factors and typically linked to HFrEF; (2) metabolic, frequently involving multiple 678

CMDs and presenting as HFpEF; (3) elderly individuals, often with AF; and (4) young, obese 679

individuals with minimal comorbidities. In parallel, recent advances have moved beyond 680

traditional unifactorial disease models, emphasizing the development of preclinical models that 681

capture the diverse clinical subtypes of HF and its associated comorbidities116,136. In the 682

following section, we focus on the multifactorial animal models in above-mentioned clinical HF 683

subtypes with different comorbidity patterns. 684

Ischemic Phenotype in HFrEF 685

Ischemic heart disease (IHD) is still arguably the most common etiology of HF, accounting for 686

approximately 40% of cases worldwide146,147. Clinically, patients with ischemic HF are often 687

male and frequently have risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and 688

peripheral artery disease. They are more likely to present with HFrEF and have a lower 689

prevalence of CKD143,145. Although myocardial infarction (MI) in patients is commonly caused 690

by the abrupt rupture, or erosion, of atherosclerotic plaques resulting from chronic cholesterol 691

accumulation, most animal models of MI involve only the surgical occlusion of the coronary 692

artery, absent the presence of chronic comorbidities or underlying genetic predispositions116. The 693

main surgical protocol to induce I/R or chronic MI in animals is coronary ligation, although 694

catheter-based approaches and coronary embolism are also choices116. To mimic multimorbid 695

conditions in patients with chronic ischemic HF, surgical-, diet-induced, or genetic animal 696

models can be performed in combination. 697

698

Models of Ischemic HF with CMDs 699

Various methods have been validated for inducing common CMDs such as hypertension, 700

diabetes, and obesity in animal models. These include dietary approaches (e.g., high-fat diet, 701

Western diet, or high-fat high-sugar diet), surgical techniques (e.g., TAC), pharmacological 702

agents (e.g., Ang II, streptozotocin [STZ]), and the use of mutant animals (e.g., Apoe or Ldlr- 703

knockout mice). These are used in combination with coronary artery ligation to mimic 704

comorbidities in ischemic HF116. For example, mice treated with STZ followed by coronary 705

ligation may mimic ischemic HF in patients with diabetes148,149, mice undergoing TAC surgery 706

followed by MI manifested more severe adverse myocardial remodeling and pronounced 707

HFrEF150. An animal model of cardiorenal syndrome was developed using coronary ligation in 708

spontaneously hypertensive rats combined with unilateral nephrectomy151. However, the report 709

did not provide detailed methodological information, imposing potential challenges in 710

reproducing the model. 711

712

Whereas combining MI with a single comorbidity is common, integrating multiple comorbidities 713

or surgeries into a single model remains rare. This is primarily due to the high mortality rates and 714

the complex interplay among them, which can complicate analysis of the experimental findings 715

and make it challenging to parse specific effects of each factor. 716


<!-- Page 18 -->


717

Models of Ischemic HF with Hyperlipidemia and Atherosclerosis 718

Apoe-knockout mice152 and Ldlr-knockout mice153 develop hyperlipidemia and spontaneous 719

atherosclerotic plaques when fed a high-fat diet (HFD)154. When subjected to chronic coronary 720

ligation, they serve as a model to study MI in the context of pre-existing hyperlipidemia and 721

atherosclerosis154. Similar animal strains include MI-prone WHHL rabbits (WHHLMI)155 and 722

SR-B1/LDLR double knockout mice156. These models mimic arterial atherosclerosis in patients, 723

spontaneous MI and peripheral artery disease (PAD). However, atherosclerosis develops slowly, 724

with heart attacks occurring after multiple months, and the variable heart damage that is induced 725

can lead to inconsistent phenotypes. 726

727

HFpEF with Multiple Cardiometabolic Comorbidities 728

Comparable to clinical phenotypes observed in patients, HFpEF models usually involve 2 or 729

more comorbidities centering around obesity and insulin resistance. Recent multifactorial models 730

have shown great promise for mimicking clinical complexity, and yet the models to date target- 731

specific HFpEF phenotypes, failing to capture the full heterogeneity of the HFpEF population. 732

Importantly, a perfect ‘one-size-fits-all’ preclinical model does not exist. Using diagnostic 733

criteria scores for patients, such as the H2FPEF126 and HFA-PEFF125, may help with validating 734

HFpEF models127,136. 735

736

Models of Unhealthy Lifestyle-induced CMDs 737

In preclinical models, unhealthy dietary patterns are mimicked by a HFD (>60% daily caloric 738

intake from fat) or by a Western diet (daily caloric intake of 36% fat and 36% sucrose). Utilizing 739

wild-type mice, rather than transgenic or strain-specific models, allows for a more accurate 740

representation of the general population with unhealthy lifestyles. Diet-based animal models 741

provide valuable insights into HF and associated CMDs in a broad context. However, severe 742

diabetes and advanced organ dysfunction are less commonly observed. 743

744

(1) HFD + L-NAME mice 745

The “two-hit” model replicates key lifestyle factors and clinical features associated with this 746

complex condition in humans142,157, exhibiting lung congestion, reduced exercise capacity, and 747

contractile dysfunction detected by GLS, and LV diastolic dysfunction. Importantly, this model 748

also mimics the genetic and molecular pathway alterations frequently observed in human HFpEF 749

hearts, including nitrosative stress-induced microvascular dysfunction driven by impaired nitric 750

oxide synthase activity. Additional comorbidities, including hypertension, obesity and pre- 751

diabetes are also present in this model. Moreover, AF, a prevalent occurrence in HF, is inducible 752

in 80% of cases in this model, coupled with left atrial enlargement, further mimicking human 753

patients158. However, young female mice manifest modest resistance to developing significant 754

LVDD, as indicated by minimal changes in echocardiographic indices, absence of cardiac 755

hypertrophy or fibrosis, lack of pulmonary congestion, stable natriuretic peptide levels, and no 756

detectable molecular alterations159. 757

758

(2) HFD + Ang II mice 759

Other co-morbidity combinations include HFD and Ang II infusion, triggering obesity, 760

hypertension, glucose intolerance, concentric hypertrophy with fibrosis, LVDD, and preserved 761

FS160-162. However, HF signs and symptoms appear to be mild, especially lacking lung 762


<!-- Page 19 -->


congestion, and the impact on exercise capacity remains unclear. Withaar et al. additionally 763

incorporated aging into this model by subjecting old mice (18-22 months) to HFD plus Ang II 764

infusion, resulting in a more typical HFpEF phenotype including the manifestations observed in 765

the young cohort but with lung congestion and decreased exercise capacity129. 766

767

(3) HFD + DOCP + aging mice 768

A combination of aging (16-month-old mice), long-term HFD (13 months) and 3 months of 769

desoxycorticosterone pivalate (DOCP) has been shown in one study to exhibit typical HFpEF 770

features including LVDD and hypertrophy, as well as multiple comorbidities including 771

hypertension, obesity, and pre-diabetes163. 772

773

(4) Western diet (WD) + DOCA + Ang II infusion 774

This combination of treatments has been established in female pigs, eliciting LVDD and 775

metabolic dysfunction including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and metabolic inflammation. 776

Nevertheless, this model has not been tested in rodents, and reproduction in these species is 777

needed164. 778

779

(5) High-Fat, High-Sucrose (HFHS) models 780

HFHS has been employed to induce obesity, diabetes, and insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, 781

mimicking the metabolic syndrome phenotype in humans165. However, the duration of treatment 782

required is usually over 20 weeks, and yet LVDD in this model is “early-stage” or mild without 783

AF and other organ damage129. 784

785

Models of High Comorbidity Burden (HTN, DM, hyperlipidemia) 786

One model combining kidney embolization with drug- or diet-induced hypertension, 787

hypercholesterolemia, renal dysfunction, and type 2 diabetes (HC/HTN/DM) in female pigs 788

effectively replicates a broad pathological spectrum of comorbidities observed in female HFpEF 789

patients166. It also mirrors the hemodynamic parameters of LVDD, with minor changes in left 790

atrial filling pressures166,167. Similar changes were observed in another swine model combining 791

WD and aortic banding (AB)168. Notably, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH, a phenotype of 792

MASLD) was induced in this WD+AB model, a comorbidity increasingly recognized as 793

significant in HFpEF. Both models achieve the highest HFpEF risk scores but lack data from 794

male or aging animals136. The experimental timeline for these models ranges from the relatively 795

long 6 to 10 months, potentially contributing to increased research time and costs. Despite 796

limitations, these models provide promising multi-hit platforms for studying the heterogeneous 797

nature of HFpEF. 798

Unlike lean WT mice, TAC surgery in Lepob/J (ob/ob) mice with preexisting obesity manifested 799

preserved EF and LVDD, as evidenced by both echocardiographic and hemodynamic 800

measurements. This combined model169 also exhibits pronounced cardiac fibrosis, inflammation 801

and oxidative stress (reflected by elevated C-reaction protein, tumor necrosis factor alpha, 802

collagen, prothrombin, and reduced Xbp1s), consistent with the common features observed in 803

HFpEF. Whereas this model successfully replicates HFpEF comorbidities of pressure overload, 804

obesity, and diabetes, it does not incorporate other key risk factors, including aging and multi- 805

organ involvement (e.g., kidney or liver dysfunction). 806


<!-- Page 20 -->


Models Involving Renal Dysfunction 807

Renal dysfunction is frequently observed in patients with HFpEF, characterized by fluid 808

overload, elevated blood pressure, and congestion170. Apart from the previously mentioned 809

HC/HTN/DM swine model, uni-nephrectomy combined with aldosterone infusion in mice of 810

C57BL6 or FB/N background induces hypertension, lung congestion, and reduced exercise 811

capacity, although it elicits inconsistent effects on glomerular filtration rate. This model mimics 812

volume and pressure overload, triggering mechanical stretch-induced cardiac inflammation and 813

fibrosis, ultimately provoking mild-to-moderate LVDD171-173. However, the lack of other 814

comorbidities, including diabetes and obesity, limits its potential in studying HF with a high 815

comorbidity burden. The roles of female sex and aging remain unexplored. 816

817

The Zucker fatty/spontaneously hypertensive heart failure F1 hybrid Rat (ZSF1)/obese 818

rats174,175 and Dahl Salt-Sensitive (DahlSS)/obese rats176,177 are each well-established models that 819

combine obesity and hypertension. Both models exhibit evidence of LVDD and cardiac fibrosis, 820

pre-diabetes and renal dysfunction, mimicking that seen in patients with elevated comorbidity 821

burden. However, increased mortality developing after 15 weeks of intervention limits long-term 822

animal studies. 823

824

Models Involving AF/MASLD: Future Directions 825

AF - a significant, and clinically important component of HF - has not been routinely 826

incorporated into the assessment of preclinical models of HFpEF. The "two-hit" model 827

combining HFD + L-NAME elicits an 80% incidence of inducible AF, but the mechanistic 828

relationship between AF and HF remains uncertain, mirroring the complex conundrum observed 829

in human diseases (See Box 1). Another significant challenge is the limited experimental 830

incorporation of MASLD into HFpEF animal models. MASLD is increasingly recognized as a 831

key factor in cardiometabolic health, sharing comorbidity patterns, including metabolic 832

inflammation, as in clinical HFpEF, as they often coexist and exacerbate each other's 833

progression. To date, MASLD has only been evaluated in a swine model treated with a 834

combination of WD and AB. In future models, MASLD should also be considered an important 835

component of the additional comorbidities in HFpEF models. 836

837

Aging Phenotype and Young HF Populations 838

Aging is among the greatest risk factors for CVD, impacting nearly all organ systems178,179. It is 839

often not studied as an independent factor in CVD owing to multiple technical challenges and 840

confounding factors, but can be easily examined alongside other comorbidities. Whereas elderly 841

patients often present with AF as a single comorbidity in clinical settings136, animal models 842

replicating this phenotype are limited. Fischer 344 rats exhibit age-related changes across 843

multiple organs, with myocardial progression from LVDD to clinical exercise intolerance, 844

ultimately culminating in left ventricular systolic dysfunction180,181. In a study of Fischer 344 rats 845

with HFpEF, atrial pacing was used to induce AF, resulting in increased AF vulnerability182. 846

However, the impact of AF on HFpEF in these models remains insufficiently explored. 847

Similarly, SAMP8 mice develop LVDD as early as six months of age but fail to exhibit a HFpEF 848

or AF phenotype183. The old hypertensive (OHT) dog induced by renal-wrapping is also a model 849

of hypertension in older animals but lacked evidence of bona fide HFpEF184-186.  Incorporating 850

older animals, with or without additional comorbidities, or extending the follow-up period for 851


<!-- Page 21 -->


younger animals, should be considered to potentially enhance the HFpEF phenotype. However, 852

incorporation of AF in preclinical models remains a major challenge. 853

854

The young patient population with HF typically comprises obese individuals with unhealthy 855

lifestyles (sedentary, unhealthy diet, smoking, etc.) with minimal comorbidities (commonly 856

hypertension and pre-diabetes). They have milder HF symptoms, lower NT-proBNP levels and 857

lower NYHA class144,145. Thus, HFpEF models incorporating multiple CMDs will likely help 858

illuminate the important features in this phenotype. 859

860

Limitations and perspectives for preclinical models incorporating HF comorbidities 861

HF is multifactorial and a biological challenge in which comorbidities contribute critically to the 862

pathophysiology of the clinical syndrome; unfortunately, this, in turn, complicates development 863

of preclinical animal models with clinical fidelity. Unsurprisingly, no single preclinical model 864

replicates the complete clinical complexity observed in HFpEF patients. Challenges exist in 865

several aspects, including difficulties in replicating the complex interactions among multiple 866

comorbid conditions and a lack of correlation between animals and humans in the biomarkers 867

used to assess disease progression and treatment efficacy. Translational failures also result from 868

differences between animals and humans in genetic background, molecular pathways, and 869

immune mechanisms. Notably, prevalent comorbidities of HF, such as AF and NASH, are 870

typically absent in existing multi-comorbidity preclinical animal models (See Box 1). 871

872

Beyond replicating clinical parameters and biomarkers, future animal models should also 873

prioritize molecular and genetic similarities HF patients. Furthermore, leveraging multiple 874

animal models in preclinical studies and therapeutic testing is strongly encouraged to capture the 875

diversity of HF phenotypes and ensure robust evaluation of novel mechanisms and potential 876

therapeutic targets. 877

880

Existing Clinical Trials, Priorities, and Challenges of Multi-Organ Clinical Trials: A Call 881

To Action 882

883

Despite the established links between metabolic and cardiovascular pathologies, liver disease and 884

multi-morbidity remain largely underrepresented in cardiometabolic trials. For example, the 885

SELECT (Semaglutide Effects on Cardiovascular Outcomes in People with Overweight or 886

Obesity) trial showed that only 8% patients had MASLD among 17,604 patients who were 887

overweight or obese187. This is far less than would be expected as the global prevalence of 888

MASLD is approximately 30%188. Thus, many large-scale trials have either excluded patients 889

with liver diseases due to concerns over drug metabolism and elevated liver enzymes or enrolled 890

them in disproportionately low numbers93,189. Such omissions risk overlooking the role of 891

lipotoxicity and hepatic dysfunction in accelerating multi-organ injury188,190. Similarly, phase 3 892

905

As a consequence of the advent of new drugs with pleiotropic mechanisms of actions, therefore 906

mitigating common underlying CKLM mechanisms with approved or potential multiple 907

indications across the CKLM spectrum of clinical presentations, a trend toward including 908

patients with multiple comorbidities is recently seen in landmark clinical trials for patients with 909

agents have broadened their inclusion criteria to individuals who have overlapping metabolic and 911

cardiac conditions including HF, CKD, obesity, T2D, and hypertension. These trials have also 912

assessed in these trials, such as sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), glucagon- 914

antagonists (ns-MRA), may exert beneficial effects on liver diseases as well. However, patients 916

with MASLD and MASH appear disproportionately under-represented in these trials. Only 917

SUMMIT (Tirzepatide for Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Obesity) and 918

Moreover, the majority of the trials did not include any secondary endpoints relevant to other 922

comorbid conditions. 923

Priorities for Multi-organ CKM Clinical Trials: Incorporating Liver-Related Endpoints 925

926

a) Collaboration 927

To advance multi-organ clinical trials, several key priorities must be considered (Figure 4). A 928

concerted collaboration across medical specialties is necessary (cardiologists, nephrologists, 929

endocrinologists and hepatologists) to synergistically develop comprehensive trial designs that 930

reflect the interconnected nature of these diseases. This multidisciplinary approach allows for a 931

holistic understanding of patient health, moving beyond the traditional siloed view of treating 932

organs separately189. By collectively addressing uncertainties, stakeholders can navigate complex 933

regulatory landscapes and advocate for patient-centric outcomes211. 934

935

b) Patient selection 936

Multi-organ trials can be enriched by identifying patients with drivers of adverse outcomes, such 937

as those with CKM diseases and advanced fibrosis (F3 and F4)212. For instance, NITs such as 938

liver stiffness measurement (LSM) can accurately identify clinically significant portal 939

hypertension (CSPH). An LSM ≥ 25 kPa and platelets ≥ 150 × 109/L can diagnose CSPH213. 940

These NITs not only improve patient stratification but also align with the need to move away 941

from invasive liver biopsies, which have safety concerns. In typical liver trials, >10,000 patients 942

undergo biopsies to enroll just a few participants due to stringent histological criteria, resulting in 943

a significant burden on both patients and sponsor resources214,215. The MAESTRO-NASH (Phase 944

3 Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of MGL-3196 [Resmetirom] in Patients With NASH 945

and Fibrosis) trial demonstrated resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening liver fibrosis, but 946

the outcome was worsening of fibrosis which necessitated another biopsy206. This repeated 947

reliance on biopsies exposes patients to risks such as mortality of approximately 1 in 10,000, 948

morbidity including post-procedure pain in 3% of patients, and bleeding risk in 1 out of 250 949

patients216. 950

951

A potential solution for invasive tests is to design a trial in two segments; one focusing on 952

patients with cirrhosis using clinical endpoints, and another involving patients with less severe 953

MASLD using surrogate endpoints. Subsequently, these two segments are bridged across the 954

entire disease spectrum. In addition, establishing new surrogate endpoints are pivotal in this 955

context. A “reasonably likely surrogate endpoint” is defined as one supported by strong 956

mechanistic and epidemiological rationale, in which an effect on the surrogate endpoint is 957

expected to correlate with clinical benefit in clinical trials, even if sufficient clinical data for 958

validation are unavailable217. Many NITs correlate with histology (listed in section above); 959

however, histological assessments are continuous rather than discrete stages, and histology itself 960

has limitations in sensitivity and specificity. Therefore, if we link NITs to hard clinical endpoints 961

such as hepatic decompensation or death, we can achieve equivalence or superiority to histology 962

in capturing clinically meaningful benefits. 963

c) Inclusivity 965

Multi-organ trials also need to address under-representation of certain patient populations in 966

previous trials. Patients with complex comorbidities, disabilities, extremes of age, ethnic 967

minorities, and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups are often under-represented due to 968

factors such as regulatory requirements favoring local populations, poor infrastructure in certain 969

regions, and concerns over data quality218. The burden of MASLD and metabolic disease in the 970

US is largely born by the Latino Americans, with Latinos manifesting a 46% prevalence of 971

MASLD compared to 26% in Black Americans219. Black Americans are less likely to have 972

severe MASLD (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]: 0.5) compared to non-Latino Whites, whereas 973

Latinos were more than twice as likely to have severe MASLD (AOR: 2.4)219. Thus, multi-organ 974

trials must prioritize inclusivity by improving site capacity building, engaging with diverse 975

communities, and addressing linguistic and cultural barriers. Additionally, early identification of 976

multi-organ conditions and increasing accessibility of routine clinical practice can improve trial 977

relevance to a broader population. 978

979

D) Progression of disease 980

Understanding the long-term progression of diseases across different organs is crucial for 981

developing effective therapies. Multi-organ trials must study the behavior of drugs over extended 982

periods, recognizing that disease progression can vary significantly by age, severity, and 983

underlying health factors. For example, in MASLD, fibrosis progression is an important 984

determinant of mortality, with patients at fibrosis stage F3 likely to experience major adverse 985

liver outcomes within six years218,220. However, MASLD has nonlinear progression, and high 986

placebo rates are observed in clinical trials because patients can stabilize without any actual drug 987

effect188,190. This variability necessitates including multiple age strata in trials to capture the 988

onset and severity of diseases such as MAFLD and CKD, which manifest differently across age 989

groups. It is important to ensure an adequate distribution of all conditions being studied, 990

especially as liver disease may take longer to become severe. 991

E) Liver-specific endpoints 993

Integrating liver-specific endpoints into CKM trials is another key priority. Similar to the way 994

cardiovascular trials have incorporated kidney outcomes, future studies can potentially include 995

liver outcomes to develop a comprehensive cardio–kidney–liver metabolic endpoint. Including 996

liver endpoints as secondary outcomes can enhance feasibility assessments, improve patient 997

phenotyping, and refine risk stratification while building consensus among stakeholders189. 998

Historically, markers of cardiometabolic health in MASH trials have focused on lipid profiles 999

and glycemic control, with scant attention to kidney or cardiovascular markers221. A holistic 1000

approach necessitates inclusion of endpoints such as improvements in steatosis, liver enzymes 1001

(alanine transaminase [ALT] and aspartate transaminase [AST]), fibrosis scores (Fibrosis-4 [FIB- 1002

4] Index, enhanced liver fibrosis [ELF] score, PRO-C3), liver stiffness measurements, and rates 1003

of portal hypertension development based on Baveno criteria189. Safety endpoints should also 1004

encompass liver-specific events, including overt hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, variceal 1005

bleeding, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score 1006

≥15, and liver-related death. 1007

Utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can improve patient 1010

representation and endpoint prediction based on biomarkers. AI-enabled electrocardiograms 1011

incorporating clinical demographic data, such as diabetes status, BMI, sex, age, and ALT levels, 1012

0.76222. Similarly, a ML model was used which predicted primary endpoints such as progression 1014

G) Data sharing 1021

Improving data-sharing practices is also a key priority to accelerate development in multi-organ 1022

clinical trials. Sponsors often face challenges due to risk-averse gatekeepers such as legal and 1023

privacy experts, leading to reluctance in sharing trial data224,225. To overcome this inertia, 1024

establishing standards that ensure downstream research utility including interoperability, 1025

transparency, and reproducibility is essential226. Regulatory acceptance of supplemental and 1026

external controls in confirmatory trials can encourage sponsors to share anonymized data, 1027

facilitating secondary analyses and further enhance the robustness of findings. 1028

H) External placebo database 1030

Multi-organ trials can have an arduously long follow-up which makes patient retention 1031

challenging for sponsors due to resource constraints, hesitancy toward biopsy requirements, 1032

uncertainty among clinicians, and sicker patients dropping out earlier. Thus, these trials may 1033

benefit by establishing an external placebo database. These databases can alleviate the burden on 1034

patients and sponsors by reducing the need for large placebo groups. Innovative trial designs 1035

such as master protocols, including basket, and platform trials, offer opportunities to investigate 1036

Whereas these trials require considerable up-front planning with significant financial backing, 1038

run229. In platform trials, a master protocol is used to facilitate the simultaneous investigation of 1040

multiple interventions are compared against a single placebo, as it reduces the overall sample 1043

size needed without compromising inferential power227,228. Similarly, basket trials involve a 1044

single drug but enroll patients with multiple subtypes of a disease and enhance inferences by 1045

Challenges of Multi-organ CKLM Clinical Trials 1050

1051

While multi-organ trials can generate meaningful evidence, they also face several challenges 1052

(Figure 5). One major challenge is that identifying appropriate patients with multi-organ disease 1053

is inherently complex. Traditional risk assessment tools, such as the Pooled Cohort Equations 1054

(PCE), do not account for the presence and severity of liver disease, which significantly impacts 1055

cardiovascular outcomes, morbidity, and mortality in patients with MASLD or MASH. For 1056

example, in 698 patients with MASLD from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis), 1057

PCE was suboptimal (AUROC: 0.67), predominantly underestimating risk in women within the 1058

lower to intermediate risk categories of MASLD229. Consequently, accurately identifying and 1059

stratifying such patients necessitates the collection of additional data and endpoints which 1060

increases the complexity and cost of multi-organ trials. 1061

1062

Incorporating patients with liver disease into cardiovascular and kidney trials is often met with 1063

hesitation due to concerns about drug metabolism and safety profiles. Many investigational drugs 1064

are metabolized in the liver, and patients with hepatic impairment may have altered 1065

pharmacokinetics which heightens the risk of adverse effects or hepatotoxicity189. This 1066

necessitates additional monitoring which complicates trial design and puts additional burden on 1067

the sponsor. The lack of standardized clinical guidelines for managing patients with overlapping 1068

conditions leads to variable treatment approaches and introduces heterogeneity into clinical 1069

trials. Patients with multi-organ diseases may receive different therapies based on local practices, 1070

specialist preferences, confusing and overlapping plans of care. This variability can confound 1071

trial results, making it challenging to attribute outcomes to the study drug rather than differences 1072

in standard care. 1073

1074

Traditional biopsy-based approaches for diagnosing and staging liver disease have a high screen 1075

failure rate of 70–90%. This means that for a trial aiming to enroll 1,000 patients, potentially 1076

>10,000 individuals may need to undergo liver biopsies. Given the serious morbidity and 1077

complication rate associated with liver biopsies, where ~1 patient may experience a near-death 1078

event per 1,000 procedures, this approach poses ethical concerns and contributes to patient 1079

reluctance to participate230. These liver biopsies are seldom used in routine clinical practice, 1080

primarily reserved for cases with diagnostic ambiguity, and are not recommended as standard 1081


<!-- Page 26 -->


diagnostic tools unless absolutely necessary94,231. Moreover, it may take up to five years to 1082

demonstrate any reduction in cirrhosis progression and even longer to observe changes in clinical 1083

events, making biopsy-based approaches impractical for timely trial outcomes. 1084

1085

Establishing consensus on developing and validating clinically meaningful organ-specific 1086

efficacy and safety endpoints remains a contentious issue. For example, while liver biochemical 1087

tests or the FIB-4 index could be included in cardiovascular or kidney trials from a hepatology 1088

perspective, significant investment in liver-specific biomarkers is unlikely until there is a 1089

universally accepted case definition based on NITs232. Currently, there is no agreement on which 1090

NITs should be used, despite substantial investments and research in this area93,189. This lack of 1091

consensus hinders the ability to define meaningful changes in NITs and their clinical benefits, 1092

creating barriers to integrating liver endpoints into multi-organ trials. The different NITs have 1093

varying limitations; for instance, the FIB-4 score performs poorly in individuals over 65 years 1094

old and those with T2D, and has a high coefficient of variation. The ELF score offers better 1095

prognostic value with less variability but may not be widely accessible or cost-effective. 1096

Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is considered the gold standard but is expensive and 1097

not feasible outside of specialized settings. 1098

1099

Defining the optimal combination of biomarkers, imaging modalities, and hard clinical outcomes 1100

also remains a challenge. Future trials must balance the need for comprehensive data with the 1101

need to minimize the burden on patients, investigators, and sponsors. Currently, there are no 1102

candidate NITs that can serve as fully validated surrogate endpoints because we lack therapies 1103

that have demonstrated definitive clinical benefits, such as reducing the need for liver 1104

transplantation or preventing liver-related mortality233. Without such therapies, it is difficult to 1105

validate NITs as predictors of meaningful clinical outcomes. Additionally, measurement 1106

inconsistencies including variability in hemoglobin A1c levels or fluctuations in liver fibrosis 1107

assessments on different days can further complicate the use of these biomarkers. While NITs are 1108

used in clinical practice due to the impracticality of biopsies, their limitations must be 1109

acknowledged, and more robust validation is necessary to enhance their utility in trials. 1110

1111

The regulatory approval processes can be complex in multi-organ trials, particularly when these 1112

trials span various medical specialties and require the green light from multiple regulatory 1113

bodies. This extends trial timelines and complicate trial execution. Global trials impose a high 1114

workload on participating sites due to differing regulations, ethical considerations, and reporting 1115

requirements across countries. Many sites, especially in resource-limited settings, lack the 1116

infrastructure and skilled workforce necessary for complex trials, particularly those involving 1117

advanced imaging234. Heterogeneity in the standard of care and variability in the use of NITs 1118

across regions adds further complexity. To address these challenges, lessons from well-developed 1119

sites can be applied to less-resourced settings, and global collaborations can enhance trial 1120

conduct. Investing in capacity building, training local healthcare professionals, home testing-kits, 1121

and leveraging mobile health units to reach remote patients can improve recruitment and 1122

retention in these trials. 1123

1124

Lastly, uncertainty surrounds the benefits of enriching trials with patients who have multiple 1125

comorbidities. While enriching CKM trials to include patients with coexisting MASLD could 1126

provide multiple indications from one trial, it raises concerns about logistics, generalizability, 1127


<!-- Page 27 -->


and statistical considerations such as control of type I error. Enrichment of this kind can also 1128

increase the burden on patients and trial sites, elevate costs, and complicate the interpretation of 1129

data. It is also possible that including patients with advanced CKM disease may make it difficult 1130

to observe liver reversibility, as the disease may have progressed beyond the point where 1131

interventions are most effective. Conversely, focusing on patients earlier in their disease 1132

progression might not capture the full spectrum of disease interactions which is necessary to 1133

understand multi-organ effects. Hence, this necessitates a delicate balance between 1134

pathophysiological understanding and practical trial design. 1135

Designing CKLM Multi-organ Clinical Trials 1137

1138

1) Selecting the Appropriate Trial Population 1139

Selecting the right patient population and determining the optimal trial duration is the first step in 1140

designing multi-organ clinical trials (Figure 6). It is essential to choose participants whose 1141

disease severity is modifiable and whose biomarkers are expected to respond to the treatment 1142

(e.g., FIB-4). For example, patients with fibrosis stages F2 or F3 may be suitable, but these 1143

conditions often progress slowly, making it challenging to detect hard endpoints within a 1144

reasonable timeframe. In such cases, incorporating composite events or surrogate markers can 1145

enhance feasibility. Patients with varying demographics must be included. Patients with 1146

subclinical diseases with sufficient level of modifiability must be included as it is possible that 1147

we might not detect many changes in a patient with F2 fibrosis who only presents with 1148

cardiovascular, kidney, or metabolic risk factors235. 1149

1150

When selecting a trial population, we must also consider practicality and retention. For patients 1151

with HFpEF who are already scheduled for imaging, it is efficient to extend these sessions by 15 1152

minutes to gather comprehensive multi-organ data. These data can include liver elastography, 1153

kidney T1-mapping or contrast MRI, cardiac measurements such as ventricular volumes and 1154

function, strain, or mitral valve flow, and body composition analysis. These evaluations can 1155

typically be completed in less than 45 minutes. Advanced AI-based segmentation can further 1156

delineate intramuscular and intermuscular fat, epicardial fat, liver fat, and other tissue 1157

compartments. Beyond standard imaging, trials might also assess substrate utilization, 1158

myocardial efficiency, perfusion reserve, fibrogenesis across multiple organs, and insulin 1159

sensitivity. Thus, including such a cohort favors practicality by minimizing burden on patients. 1160

1161

Achieving equitable representation in multi-organ clinical trials is also crucial for enhancing 1162

health outcomes and understanding sex- and ethnicity-specific treatment effects. The prevalence 1163

of male-only principal investigators and recruitment strategies that fail to actively refer women 1164

to specialized care settings have further diminished female participation. Additionally, many 1165

exclusion criteria lack strong justification; with data indicating that only 47.2% of 2,700 criteria 1166

were strongly justified, with most randomized controlled trials containing at least one poorly 1167

justified exclusion criterion216. Addressing these issues requires evaluating the clinical necessity 1168

of criteria, minimizing unnecessary restrictions, and considering implicit biases. 1169

1170

Selection of appropriate patients for multi-organ clinical trials can also be enhanced by 1171

leveraging advanced biomarkers and imaging modalities that provide a comprehensive 1172

understanding of disease burden and progression. For example, the SomaSignal Assay, which 1173


<!-- Page 28 -->


requires only a simple blood draw, can offer deeper insights into clinical trial populations, as 1174

demonstrated in the PIVENS (Placebo for Treatment of Nonalcoholic FaWy Liver Disease) 1175

study236. Similarly, imaging techniques such as LiverMultiScan yield quantitative measures of 1176

liver fat, inflammation, and iron content237. For discriminating any healthy individuals with any 1177

degree of fibrosis, steatosis, or iron content, LiverMultiScan showed an AUROC of 0.94 (p < 1178

0.0001, 95% CI 0.90–0.99), 0.93 (95% CI 0.87–0.99, p < 0.0001), and 0.94 (95% CI 0.87–1.00, 1179

p < 0.0001), respectively238. CoverScan extends this concept to multiple organs, measuring fat, 1180

inflammation, and function across organ systems, thus enabling a more precise stratification of 1181

cardiovascular risk in multi-organ disease states239. These tools are particularly well suited to 1182

multi-organ clinical trials due to their predictive capabilities for assessing cardiovascular residual 1183

risks, hospitalizations due to HF, changes in kidney function, and glycemic control. Hence, this 1184

not only captures the complexity of multi-organ disease but also refines patient selection, risk 1185

stratification, and outcome prediction in clinical trials. 1186

2) Baseline Characteristics and Outcomes 1188

Multi-organ clinical trials need to meticulously document detailed clinical profiles, including 1189

cardiovascular, kidney, liver, and metabolic parameters, at baseline and to reassess this over time 1190

(Table 3). For cardiovascular assessments, this might involve echocardiography, measuring atrial 1191

strain, NT-proBNP and BNP levels, and monitoring variables such as blood pressure, cardiac 1192

troponins, inflammatory and collagen biomarkers, as well as exercise capacity, using the 6- 1193

minute walk test (6MWT). Kidney function should be characterized by the UACR, baseline 1194

eGFR measurements, and subsequent assessments of eGFR slope. Metabolic status can be 1195

assessed using parameters such as hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), BMI, and lipid profile tests. 1196

Patient-reported outcomes provide invaluable insights into the quality of life and symptom 1197

burden in multi-organ conditions. Instruments such as the EuroQol-5D, Kansas City 1198

Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ), Chronic Liver Disease Questionnaire, and NASH 1199

CHECK can provide crucial information about patient experiences and functional impairments 1200

that go beyond traditional clinical metrics189. 1201

1202

Multi-organ trials can also include advanced imaging modalities for phenotyping and endpoint 1203

determination. Cardiac MRI can provide insights into ejection fraction, myocardial strain, 1204

ventricular volumes, left ventricular (LV) mass, extracellular volume through T1 mapping, 1205

epicardial fat, and arterial stiffness measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based pulse 1206

wave velocity, capturing subtle structural and functional changes in the heart240. Additionally, 1207

integrating kidney injury biomarkers such as clusterin, cystatin-C, KIM-1, NGAL, NAG, and 1208

osteopontin can refine risk stratification and improve early intervention strategies85. 1209

Comprehensive case report forms should include these data to ensure robust baseline 1210

phenotyping and facilitate the holistic understanding of each patient’s condition through detailed 1211

medication histories, documentation of pre-existing vascular events, and characterization of 1212

arrhythmias, valvular disorders, and any previous interventions. It is also crucial to carefully 1213

define and longitudinally adjudicate any inpatient or outpatient cardiovascular, kidney, or liver- 1214

related events. 1215

Composite endpoints are also warranted in multi-organ trials, which include events that are 1217

relatively similar in their clinical importance to patients, biologically and mechanistically related, 1218

and influenced in a concordant way by the therapy. Typically, a hierarchy of endpoints might 1219

start with severe outcomes such as cardiac death at the top, followed by hospitalization for HF 1220

and kidney failure. While including softer events or surrogate endpoints might boost statistical 1221

power, this approach can also complicate the interpretation of results. Alternatively, win-ratio 1222

analysis provides a more nuanced comparison by ranking patients according to clinical priority 1223

outcomes such as death, liver cancer, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), major 1224

adverse liver events (MALE), or the necessity for a liver biopsy241. In shorter, phase 1 or 2 trials, 1225

focusing on surrogate efficacy measures for both the liver (e.g., MRI-based proton density fat 1226

fraction [PDFF], vibration-controlled transient elastography [VCTE]-based controlled 1227

attenuation parameter [CAP] scores, serum biomarkers, or MRI-based fibrosis indices) and other 1228

organs can guide critical decisions. Imaging-based assessments of steatosis or fibrosis and 1229

caution is advised as techniques like VCTE may overestimate congestion in cardiac patients. By 1231

strategically integrating baseline phenotyping, advanced imaging, tailored biomarker panels, 1232

patient-reported outcomes, and clearly defined composite or surrogate endpoints, multi-organ 1233

clinical trials can provide a more thorough and clinically relevant evaluation of novel therapies. 1234

3) Meaningful Evidence 1236

There is a need to establish a consensus on what constitutes convincing evidence in multi-organ 1237

clinical trials. The key question in the context of multi-organ trials is how to design, execute, and 1238

interpret successful clinical trials that incorporate a multiplicity of endpoints. One potential 1239

approach is to employ causal inference frameworks in the design, execution, and interpretation 1240

of such complex trials to provide a systematic, step-by-step approach to pre-specifying study 1241

design and analysis plans242. Multi-organ clinical trials can encounter unique challenges, such as 1242

stringent regulatory requirements, lengthy follow-up periods for clinical endpoints, competing 1243

risks, invasive surrogate measures, and heterogeneous patient populations. To manage these 1244

complexities, innovative frameworks like the “Flexible Augmented Clinical Trial for Improved 1245

eVidence gEneration” (FACTIVE) have been developed243. FACTIVE designs bridge 1246

conventional phase III trials to a broader population, or different experimental conditions, that 1247

can be tailored to address a particular question243. FACTIVE enhances a core randomized trial by 1248

generating rigorous efficacy and safety data while integrating real-world elements typical of 1249

clinical practice. Briefly, FACTIVE design merges elements of a traditional randomized 1250

controlled trial with those of a real-world study243. Initially, FACTIVE sets up a core trial 1251

conducted under strict experimental conditions. This traditional segment serves as a rigorous 1252

control and minimizes variables that could affect the outcome. Concurrently, FACTIVE expands 1253

by incorporating an augmented part that includes real-world elements. This part of the trial is 1254

tailored to more closely resemble clinical practice, with a broader patient population and varied 1255

healthcare settings typical of routine clinical care243. This dual structure enables FACTIVE to 1256

produce robust evidence that is both scientifically valid and broadly applicable. 1257

4) Interim Analysis 1259

In large and complex multi-organ clinical trials, interim analysis can play a pivotal role. It can 1260

help maintain objectivity, optimize resource allocation, and ensure that the focus remains on 1261

meaningful clinical objectives rather than purely commercial aims244. The use of Bayesian 1262

methods, such as predictive probability, offers a robust framework for interim decision- 1263

making245. These methods allow for the synthesis of prior knowledge with real-time data 1264

accumulation to estimate the probability of achieving the trial’s ultimate success. Such predictive 1265


<!-- Page 30 -->


insights are invaluable, enabling sponsors and investigators to make critical decisions about 1266

continuing, modifying, or prematurely terminating a trial. This not only helps in conserving 1267

resources and reducing costs but also focuses efforts on interventions that are most likely to 1268

succeed in meeting their primary endpoints. This provides the ability to achieve reliable and 1269

clinically relevant outcomes in the challenging arena of multi-organ clinical trials. 1270

Evolving clinical practice toward a multi-organ, multi-disciplinary integrated care 1272

approach: focus on liver disease. 1273

1274

Every healthcare professional, whether primary care doctors or specialists, will encounter 1275

patients with metabolic risk factors who are at risk for MASLD and cardiovascular disease. 1276

Therefore, screening and diagnosis of MASLD, and cardiovascular diseases require a multi- 1277

disciplinary approach. Currently, it not recommended to screen for liver steatosis among the 1278

general population level. However, cardiologists should consider screening for MASLD in 1279

patients incidentally noted for hepatic steatosis and metabolic risk factors. NITs like FIB-4, 1280

which is based on platelet count, age, AST, and ALT, can be utilized for initial risk assessment. 1281

An FIB-4 score <1.3 suggests a low likelihood of advanced fibrosis and rules out severe fibrosis. 1282

Conversely, FIB-4 score >2.67, adjusted for age, indicates a high probability of advanced fibrosis 1283

and is associated with a 40% increase in cardiovascular mortality246. High or indeterminate FIB- 1284

4 scores should prompt further assessments using imaging techniques like VCTE or a referral to 1285

hepatology for more detailed staging of disease and fibrosis. The effectiveness of FIB-4 1286

diminishes significantly outside the age range of 35 to 65 years247. Therefore, relying on a single 1287

NIT may not adequately identify those at risk of fibrosis and cirrhosis. Hence, cardiologists may 1288

use a combination of ≥2 NITs, including serum- or imaging-based biomarkers, to accurately 1289

stage and stratify risk in patients with a FIB-4 score >1.3. 1290

Hepatologists also have an important role in screening and mitigating cardiovascular risk 1291

in patients with MASLD. Hepatologists should consider annual screening for common risk 1292

factors, such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and obesity. This may be assessed via 1293

tools such as the PREVENT (Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events) calculator, 1294

which predicts 10- and 30-year risks of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and HF 1295

by including metabolic comorbidities and CKD248. For patients with advanced MASLD, 1296

coronary artery calcium may also be assessed. Additionally, clinicians should look for signs of 1297

any structural abnormalities, such as LV hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and valvular 1298

calcifications, in symptomatic patients with MASLD. 1299

General practitioners (GPs) also have an important role in an integrated care approach. 1300

GPs frequently manage T2DM, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, alcohol use disorders and obesity, 1301

and thus are ideally positioned to identify and manage the population at risk of MASLD. For 1302

initial MASLD screening in these patients, GPs could consider liver ultrasound to assess for 1303

hepatic steatosis and subsequently utilize NITs like FIB-4, which require minimal resources and 1304

are suitable for widespread use in population screening. Early screening can ensure quick 1305

referrals and coordinated care with specialists like cardiologists and hepatologists. GPs can also 1306

assist in long-term disease screening. For example, in high risk populations, such as those with 1307

T2D or established cardiovascular disease, GPs may perform FIB-4 annually, while in low risk 1308

populations, such as younger populations with fewer cardiovascular risk factors, FIB-4 screening 1309

every two years may be sufficient249. 1310

Conclusion 1312

Our review sets out to underline an urgent need to consider the inter-organ crosstalk basis of HF 1313

and CKLM disease today in its totality. Notwithstanding all the challenges discussed, we need to 1314

consider how clinical trials can be conducted to include a broader cohort of patients with multi- 1315

organ diseases, and preclinical disease models can be selected to reflect current disease 1316

complexity. Clinical trials and preclinical disease models so designed may facilitate the efficient 1317

identification of therapies that benefit patients across multiple disease domains, aligning with 1318

real-world clinical settings (See Box 1). Collectively, for clinical trials, this also warrants a call 1319

to reduce reliance on invasive tests, develop reasonably likely surrogate endpoints, ensure 1320

broader demographic representation, and integrate AI-based tools to optimize patient selection 1321

and risk stratification. Multi-organ trials should include patients with modifiable disease, with 1322

consideration for practicality and retention, and assess comprehensive multi-organ parameters, 1323

along with a variety of endpoints. Overall, the traditional approach of HF epidemiology often 1324

focuses on individual cardiometabolic risk factors for overall HF risk. Instead, we propose a shift 1325

away from the siloed perspective and concerted systematic studies of shared mechanisms of 1326

extra-cardiac, multi-organ dysfunction.  Future research designs should integrate the concept of 1327

“common soil”, linking multi-organ readouts to comprehensively unravel the complexities of 1328

multimorbidity and heterogeneity across the clinical spectrum of HF. 1329

# Macrovascular Hemodynamics and Peripheral Perfusion in Cardiogenic Shock

**Authors:** Leah B Kosyakovsky; William B Earle; Colter Wichern; Carla Boyle; Conrad Macon; Rebecca Mathew; Benjamin Hibbert; Joaquin E Cigarroa; Jeffrey A Marbach

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Cardiovascular Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | bDivision of Cardiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | cDivision of Cardiovascular Medicine, Knight Cardiovascular Institute, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon, USA | dDivision of Cardiology, University of Ottawa Heart Institute, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada | eDepartment of Cardiovascular Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Despite significant advances in care over the past few decades, mortality among patients with cardiogenic shock (CS) remains up to 50%. Given the persistently high mortality, there is an urgent need for both better prognostic tools and treatment strategies. The pathophysiology of CS has major contributions from both macrovascular and microvascular dysfunction, but therapies are titrated toward the more readily measurable metrics (ie, mean arterial pressure, cardiac index, etc) under the assumption that both macrovascular and microvascular dynamics will respond to intervention in tandem. However, emerging evidence suggests that macrovascular and microvascular circulatory functions are not always aligned, particularly in those with critical illness. This review summarizes the significance of different macrovascular and microvascular metrics in CS, drawing from a robust field of evidence to demonstrate the promising role that microvascular tissue perfusion markers play in management of patients with CS and summarize the current understanding of this burgeoning field.

Key words: cardiogenic shock, hemodynamics, outcomes, tissue perfusion

## Abstract

## Abstract

Cardiogenic shock mortality remains high, and there’s an urgent need to improve prognostication and treatment.

The pathophysiology of cardiogenic shock is contributed to by both microvascular and macrovascular dysfunction.

Macrovascular metrics are more readily targetable, but do not fully represent tissue oxygenation and perfusion.

It is critical to also consider how to incorporate microvascular targets into cardiogenic shock management.

The macrovasculature and microvasculature serve distinct functions to maintain circulation. The macrovascular circulation, consisting of large arteries and veins, acts as a conduit for blood flow from the central circulation to peripheral tissues.1 Meanwhile, the microvascular circulation, including arterioles, capillaries, and venules, plays a crucial role in regulating blood flow and facilitating the exchange of nutrients, oxygen, and waste products. The function of these 2 systems is assumed to be closely aligned under normal physiological conditions and in critical illness. Accordingly, alterations in macrovascular hemodynamics, which are easier to quantify, are thought to be mirrored in microvascular tissue perfusion. This principle has been a cornerstone in patient management since the advent of continuous hemodynamic monitoring in the 1960s. As a result, the microvascular system’s varied and specialized functions are frequently overlooked in clinical settings, in favor of more readily apparent and quantifiable macrovascular hemodynamic data.2 Consequently, the predominant approach to managing circulatory shock, as recommended by societal guidelines and expert consensus, focuses heavily on interventions aimed at improving macrovascular hemodynamic parameters such as systemic arterial pressure, right atrial pressure, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and cardiac output (CO).3

However, emerging evidence suggests that microvascular abnormalities can persist despite apparently normal macrovascular parameters, leading to inadequate tissue oxygenation and potential organ failure. The assumption that manipulation of macrovascular parameters will inevitably be reflected in tissue perfusion must be re-examined, as the interplay between these 2 components of the cardiovascular system may be more complex than initially conceived. Herein, we will review the significance of macrovascular abnormalities in the setting of CS and explore the growing role of microvascular tissue perfusion markers in disease management (Central Illustration). By identifying gaps and limitations in our current understanding, we aim to provide insights into potential avenues for refining treatment strategies and shifting toward a more nuanced, tissue-centric approach to CS management.

Microvascular targets can offer important additional insight, including measures of global tissue perfusion, peripheral perfusion, and regional tissue oxygenation. ## Macrovascular hemodynamic targets

### Systemic arterial blood pressure

One of the cornerstones of CS management is maintaining an optimal mean arterial pressure (MAP), but the appropriate range across different shock states remains uncertain. In general, targeting a MAP between 60-65 mm Hg and/or a systolic blood pressure (SBP) of ≥90 mm Hg is recommended for CS,3 though in patients with wide pulse pressure, these MAP and SBP targets can reflect substantial differences in perfusion. However, these differences may be driven by autoregulation, which operates through the contraction and dilation of upstream arterioles in response to increases and decreases in systemic pressure, respectively.4 As there is often a lower limit of blood pressure to which an arteriole can compensate with dilation, individuals with baseline hypertension may have different thresholds for inadequate perfusion, ranging between 50 and 150 mm Hg.

Much of the evidence for MAP targets in the management of CS has been extrapolated from other forms of circulatory shock. One trial found that in patients with septic shock, targeting a relatively lower MAP (65-70 mm Hg) achieved favorable outcomes—reinforcing the supposition that targeting a MAP of 60 to 65 mm Hg in patients with CS may be reasonable.5 Burstein and colleagues evaluated this hypothesis in a single-center, retrospective analysis. Among 1,002 patients with CS, they found that patients who survived to hospital discharge had a higher mean MAP during the first 24 hours of admission compared to nonsurvivors (75 mm Hg vs 71 mm Hg; P < 0.001)6 and that those with a mean 24-hour MAP <65 mm Hg were nearly twice as likely to die in-hospital compared to a MAP >65 mm Hg (57% vs 28%; adjusted OR: 2.0; P < 0.001). No difference in outcomes was observed when patients with a mean 24-hour MAP 65 to 74 mm Hg were compared to those with a mean 24-hour MAP ≥75 mm Hg (P > 0.10).6 These findings suggest that, while MAPs below 65 mm Hg are potentially harmful, targeting MAPs above 75 mm Hg provides no additional benefit. Meanwhile, in a post hoc analysis of the DOREMI (Milrinone as Compare with Dobutamine in the Treatment of Cardiogenic Shock) trial—a randomized, double-blind trial comparing dobutamine to milrinone in patients with CS—patients with a mean MAP ≥70 mm Hg (high MAP) in the first 36 hours following randomization were compared to those with a mean MAP <70 mm Hg (low MAP).7 The combined major adverse cardiac events (MACE) outcome occurred in 42.2% vs 67.6% of patients in the high and low MAP groups, respectively (adjusted relative risk: 0.70; P = 0.01). Additionally, lower all-cause mortality was observed in the high MAP (28.9%) compared to the low MAP (57.8%) cohorts (adjusted relative risk: 0.56; P < 0.01) (Table 1).

Further complicating this issue is the occasional absence of overt hypotension in CS, as arterial pressure may be preserved in some patients with compensatory vasoconstriction with or without vasopressor agents.18

### Invasive hemodynamics

While invasive hemodynamic monitoring has been associated with reduced in-hospital mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock (CS), no prospective randomized trials have demonstrated a clear benefit in guiding care based on these parameters.19 A comprehensive review of these data has previously been published by Mathew et al and many of the key studies have been summarized in Table 1.20 Further studies, such as the ongoing PACCS (Pulmonary Artery Catheter in Cardiogenic Shock) trial (NCT05782780), are needed to establish the role of invasive hemodynamic monitoring in CS, including contributions to overall mortality as well as the restoration of macrovascular and/or microvascular perfusion.

## Clinical indices of peripheral perfusion

### Capillary refill time

Despite the development of precise invasive tools such as the arterial line and the pulmonary artery catheter, the quickest, cheapest, and simplest assessment of a patient’s peripheral perfusion continues to be the bedside physical examination, including techniques such as capillary refill time (CRT). CRT is defined as the time taken for the color to return to a peripheral capillary bed after external pressure has been sufficiently applied to result in blanching. Although a normal CRT has been variably defined since it was first formally applied in 1947, most clinicians deem a CRT of <2 to 3 seconds as normal.21

Among 61 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with CS, a prolonged CRT of more than 3 seconds was associated with increased 90-day mortality or the need for venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support (HR: 12.38; 95% CI: 2.91-52.71). Interestingly, CRT did not correlate with macrovascular parameters such as HR, SBP, cardiac index (CI), and capillary perfusion index, but increased CRT was significantly correlated with multiple microcirculatory parameters including mottling, urine output, and central venous-arterial carbon dioxide difference, indicating that CRT may provide critical insight into micro-, rather than macro-, circulatory dysfunction.22 While CRT has clinical utility as a marker of peripheral perfusion, CRT assessment may be limited by confounders such as age, temperature, ambient light, and pressure application as well as poor intraobserver and interobserver reliability.23 Thus, CRT is considered to be an adjunct means of assessment of perfusion rather than a gold standard.

### Peripheral perfusion index

An additional noninvasive measure of tissue perfusion is the peripheral perfusion index (PPI), defined as the ratio between the pulsatile and nonpulsatile component of the pulse oximetry waveform.24 Among critically ill patients with circulatory shock, there was a concordant linear correlation between the change in PPI and the core-to-toe temperature difference (R2 = 0.52; P < 0.001). A PPI of 1.4 discriminated best between a normal and abnormal core-to-toe temperature difference (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.84-0.98). To assess the prognostic valve of PPI in critically ill patients, investigators measured PPI 8 hours after early resuscitation in 202 ICU patients. They found the greatest AUC (0.835) for the prediction of 30-day mortality, outperforming ScvO2, P(v-a)CO2, and lactate.25 The combination of low ScvO2 and low PPI was associated with the lowest survival rate at 30 days, suggesting that complementary ScvO2 and PPI assessment may better identify endpoints of resuscitation and adverse patient outcomes (Table 2). There was no significant relationship between PPI and macrovascular measures including MAP, supporting its unique role in microvascular assessment. A potential limitation with PPI is that it may be less accurate in patients with severe CS, particularly those treated with mechanical circulatory support, given decreased pulsatility. In addition, PPI interpretation can be substantially limited by patient factors, such as pain, body temperature, and peripheral vascular disease, in addition to clinical factors such as disease state, which introduce substantial variation in PPI skew and threshold.37
